questions.q: To let a principal in Account A assume a role owned by Account B, what must be true?
options: Account B's role trust policy must name Account A as a trusted principal, and Account A's identity policy must allow sts:AssumeRole on that role ARN
Only Account B needs to configure anything; Account A needs no permissions of its own
Both accounts must share the same IAM user credentials
Cross-account role assumption is not possible in AWS
questions.explain: Cross-account access requires permission granted on both sides: the resource account's trust policy trusting the caller account, and the caller's own identity policy allowing the AssumeRole call.

questions.q: What is the purpose of an external ID in a cross-account trust policy?
options: A shared secret required alongside AssumeRole to prevent the confused deputy problem
A unique identifier for the S3 bucket being accessed
The AWS region where the role can be assumed
A replacement for the account ID in the Principal field
questions.explain: The external ID is a shared secret condition that must be passed alongside the AssumeRole call, closing the gap where trusting an account ID alone could be exploited by a confused deputy.

questions.q: What is the 'confused deputy problem' that the external ID pattern prevents?
options: A third party tricking a trusted, legitimate service into misusing its own valid permissions on their behalf
An IAM user forgetting their password
Two AWS accounts having the same account ID
A Lambda function timing out during execution
questions.explain: The confused deputy problem occurs when a third party manipulates a legitimately trusted service into acting on their behalf using that service's real permissions — the external ID closes this attack path.

questions.q: In the partner-delivery example, why is a cross-account role preferred over handing the partner an IAM user's access keys?
options: A role issues temporary, scoped credentials with no standing secret to leak, rather than a long-lived credential crossing a company boundary
IAM users cannot write to S3 under any circumstances
Access keys are more expensive than role assumption
Partners are technically unable to use IAM user credentials
questions.explain: A cross-account role grants scoped, temporary credentials (e.g. s3:PutObject on one prefix only) instead of handing over a long-lived access key that represents a standing secret shared across a company boundary.

questions.q: Is trusting Account A's account ID in a role's trust policy sufficient on its own for secure cross-account access?
options: It works, but adding an external ID condition is standard practice to prevent a confused deputy from misusing that trust
Yes, and no additional configuration is ever recommended
No — trust policies cannot reference external account IDs at all
No — cross-account trust always requires disabling S3 Block Public Access
questions.explain: Trusting an account ID alone can technically work, but without an external ID condition it's vulnerable to the confused deputy problem — which is why AWS recommends the external ID pattern for third-party/partner relationships.
